editorial.headline: UNA SEMANA. UN NÚMERO.
editorial.editorial:
WEEKLY existe porque internet produce demasiadas cosas interesantes como para intentar leerlas todas y demasiadas cosas absurdas como para dejar que el algoritmo decida por nosotros.

Esta revista junta las fuentes que elegiste, encuentra historias que merecen atención y las convierte en un número que se puede leer de principio a fin. No pretende ser neutral sobre lo que resulta interesante: pretende ser curiosa.

Aquí conviven videojuegos, cine, animación, tecnología, retro y todas esas cosas raras que terminan apareciendo cuando uno sigue un enlace porque decía que algo era prácticamente magia.

WEEKLY no quiere reemplazar a las fuentes originales. Quiere ser el lugar desde donde descubres qué vale la pena abrir. Cuando una historia está completa, la leemos aquí. Cuando una fuente solo permite ofrecer un resumen, te mandamos a leerla donde corresponde.

Una semana. Un número. Un montón de cosas interesantes.

Nos vemos la próxima semana.

h1: Sandra Bullock Recalls “Auditioning for Every Pervert” and Being Asked to “Drop My Pants”: “Not the Role for Me”

contentBlocks.text: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most

Sandra Bullock looked back on the duration of her career in the entertainment industry in conversation with Jennifer Aniston for Interview magazine, where she recalled making a decision that she did not want to take on roles that required her to audition for “perverts” who would ask her to “drop my pants.”

The Practical Magic 2 star chatted with her dear friend, the Friends actress, for Interview ‘s Tuesday cover. They discussed Bullock’s return to the big screen, why the Practical Magic sequel is a “love letter” to Bullock’s own daughter and navigating life in the public eye. Related Stories Movies 'Practical Magic 2' Leads Box Office as 'Spider-Man' Eyes All-Time Domestic Record Movies 'Practical Magic 2' Whips Up $4.7M in Box Office Previews

Aniston asked Bullock if there was a “moment when you made a deliberate choice about the kind of career you wanted, or did it just evolve?” The Oscar winner cited a time when she was living in New York, working as a waitress.

“I was auditioning for every pervert that existed, asking me to drop my pants. I was like, ‘Nope, not the role for me,'” Bullock said. “I was working my way up. Every working actor thinks you will never work again so you just take what you can get and make the most of it.”

She added that “the only time I was intentional about my career” was when she decided to pivot away from rom-coms. “I said, ‘I need to stop right now with the rom-coms,’ because I was getting so much shit for them. And I took a role in this film called Crash ,” Bullock said.

Crash would go on to win the Oscar for best picture in 2006; four years later, in one of her most renowned dramatic roles, Bullock won the Academy Award for best actress for her performance in The Blind Side .
Bullock is currently starring in Practical Magic 2 , which released Friday, marking her first film in four years. She last appeared in 2022’s The Lost City with Channing Tatum.
The sequel grossed $13 million domestically on Friday, including Thursday previews . Practical Magic 2 is likely heading to an opening weekend of around or just under $30 million.

Automattic confirms Mullenweg has returned as CEO after attempted ouster by board

After a tumultuous week, which saw WordPress founder Matt Mullenweg ousted from his position as CEO of Automattic , WordPress.com’s parent company, by way of a board vote, the company has now issued a statement confirming that Mullenweg has returned to his position.

“Matt Mullenweg is the chairman and CEO of Automattic, with full support of the board and if you search online you can see many top executives and Automatticians supporting him as well,” a company spokesperson shared with TechCrunch via email just after 5 PM ET on Saturday evening. articles.title: StarCraft Devs Promise New Game Will Definitely Release in 2030
articles.description: We got the chance to speak with the developers of the new StaCcraft game, who explained why they shared such a distant release date and even teased some potential gameplay elements.

h1: StarCraft Devs Promise New Game Will Definitely Release in 2030
h2: They also teased potential gameplay elements.

contentBlocks.text: We got the chance to speak with the developers of the new StarCraft game, who explained why they shared such a distant release date and even teased some potential gameplay elements for this highly-anticipated title.

StarCraft is finally getting a new game, and it’s taking a drastically different approach from its predecessors; instead of an RTS, Blizzard’s grisly sci-fi property is making its debut in the realm of open-world shooters, and it’s set to launch in 2030.

That’s a long way out from now, and it’s anyone’s guess as to what the world will look like in four years. We got the chance to ask the developers everyone’s burning question at Blizzcon 2026: Why announce the game if there’s still so much time left before it releases?
StarCraft First-look Images
Dan Hay, GM & VP of StarCraft and AnaLee Haertling, Associate Director, told us that sharing a firm release date helps keep them “honest” — and yes, 2030 is a firm release date.

“You walk a funny line, because it’s like, you wanna tease, and we wanna say, ‘Hey, this is where we wanna land,’” Hay explained. “The reason why I love a really good date, is because the reality is that it puts a target. It allows us to say to a team that that’s what we’re going for. It’s a rallying cry, and we’re focused on that. We wanna make sure we deliver something that is fun, something that is powerful, and something that allows you to explore. But I also like the idea that there’s a frame that keeps us honest. And it says, ‘2030, let’s go.’”
When asked if 2030 was a solid date, Hay confirmed that it is, indeed, “solid.”

While Hay couldn’t tell us how long the game has been in development, he did share some insight into how hard the team is working to transform StarCraft into a world that feels like a living, breathing universe that’s both welcoming to new players and recognizable to longtime fans.

“I can’t tell you how long it’s been in development with the team, but I can tell you how long it’s been in development in my head, and it’s probably about 25 years,” he joked. “For us, I think what’s important is that we've gone out to find people who really love the brand. We’ve gone out to people who know the brand, who come back and really feel the love of the legacy. We’ve taken great pains and great care to make something that feels authentic, that when you walk through this world, you recognize it.

“It's a tricky thing. It’s a bit of a knife’s edge. You wanna build something that is welcoming and inviting to new players but you wanna make sure it feels real. That when you walk into a bar it feels like a bar from the original world. When you meet players and characters and you see them, they've got the weapons and the armor and it feels authentic and it feels real.”

Hay went on to drop a few subtle hints at what players can expect in this new game, saying that StarCraft will bring into sharp focus the rough edges of its world, along with the visceral feeling of being a soldier fighting against massive, deadly creatures.

“We wanna show that it’s rough tools out there, it's a difficult world, it's filled with warfare and different factions and different groups of people, and they don’t always get along, and we wanted to bring that to bear from the very beginning,” he told us.

“When you think about what StarCraft will allow you to do, and we thought about how we tell this story — this is the way to tell that story. To be boots on the ground, to be down in the muck and the dirt, and to feel the tension of it.

“There was something really powerful — and I have to be careful not to give too much away here — I remember seeing the first time that a Hydralisk was 10 feet tall, and it was basically snapping at me. And I’ve got a gun and I’ve got armor, and I’m feeling like I’m down in the dirt and I’m feeling the weight of it. Emily was just talking about the deployment of the barracks. What’s super powerful about it is the moment you drop down on the ground, your perspective changes. It doesn’t feel like you’re a god looking down at this and you’re detached. It feels like, ‘My God, I'm in the middle of this. Every decision matters. Everything I do feels like it has gravitas.’”

He also dove into why Blizzard chose to take StarCraft in such a wildly different direction, rather than staying with the series’ RTS roots — and in doing so, shed some light on a few possible key gameplay elements, one of which is using an enemy as a “tool” against another enemy.

“For us, when we think about the themes and we think about the opportunity for you to be on the battlefield and for you to go out and think about the vista, the opportunity to explore, and then to discover, and then to disrupt. It’s incredibly unique. And then when you think about the different factions that there are, we just wanted people to go out into these worlds and actually get a sense of what it’s like to meet these different groups.

“Again, I really wanna talk about this stuff, but I also have to hold some stuff back, but what's really important is you think about some of these different factions in StarCraft, and you think about what they bring and you think about the way that it feels. I have imagery in my head right now that I can be careful not to describe, but I’m seeing an awful lot of biomass, and I’m seeing a lot of stuff we were hinting at. If you look at the teaser and you start to see that moment where the barracks is flying in and you look at the planet, you’ll actually see all the things that are alive on that planet and get a sense of that feel.

“For us, it felt right to put you down on the ground in the middle of people that are fighting and they don’t agree. This feeling of, ‘The enemy of my enemy is a tool to be used.’ We felt like the open world and the opportunity to explore and to discover and of course to disrupt and to use my enemy against another enemy felt really powerful.”

StarCraft is still a ways out, but you can catch up on all the other exciting news Blizzard had to offer in our round-up blog for the event's Opening Ceremony and take a peek at everything that's available to play right now.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

Alan Ritchson and his wife, Catherine Ritchson, are ending their marriage after two decades together.
The couple announced their separation Saturday in a joint message on social media, saying that their children “will always be at the center of our world.”

“After twenty years together, Cat and I have decided to end our marriage and continue alongside one another in a different way,” reads the Instagram post. “We grew up together. We built a life and a family together. And we are raising three incredible boys who will always be the center of our world.” Related Stories Movies 'Practical Magic 2' Leads Box Office as 'Spider-Man' Eyes All-Time Domestic Record Movies 'Practical Magic 2' Whips Up $4.7M in Box Office Previews
The Reacher star and Catherine share three sons.

“Nothing can diminish what these years have meant to us — or the love and respect we will always share,” the statement continued. “The best gift we can give one another — and our boys — right now is friendship, grace and a commitment to becoming the strongest co-parents we can be.”
The pair also noted that they “want to give each other room to grow into the people we are becoming,” and asked for privacy while they navigate co-parenting.
Ritchson’s rep declined further comment when reached by The Hollywood Reporter.
In a 2024 interview with THR , Ritchson opened up about how he first met Catherine while they were both in high school taking classes at a state college.

“I thought she was a college student, so I was afraid to talk to her. I figured there was no point because she’s going to be older than me, but I found out she was doing the exact same thing that I was. We finally spoke and then did a play together that summer,” he said. “We ended up dating and I was madly in love, but she also lived far enough away that when the play was over, I figured we were never going to see each other again.”
The remained friends after their initial split and reconnected years later before tying the knot in 2006.

While OpenAI has filed confidentially for an IPO , the company will not be going public this year , according to CEO Sam Altman.

h1: Retro Review: Lost Planet 3

contentBlocks.text: by Patrick Hickey Jr. | Sep 12, 2026 | 2010s , Reviews

Set 50 years before the events of the first “Lost Planet,” this game is definitely geared more towards fans of the series. At the same time, since it’s a prequel, it’s not a bad place to start for newcomers either.

If you’ve played the series before, the gameplay is similar in the fact that you’ll explore by yourself and in your mech. There’s a heck of a lot of third-person shooting to be had and if you’re the kind of gamer that enjoys the “Gears of War” series, these gameplay sections will be fun and intuitive.

While the enemies and gameplay are cool, but it’s the characters and graphics and story that’ll hook you the most. Like a James Cameron film, you’ll be taken to a far-away world with plenty of friends and unknown alien enemies. The interaction between the characters and plot development in the end is what really sets the game apart from its predecessors.

The Final Verdict: The “Avatar” inspired story is not a bad one and the mech-battling holds up well too. There isn’t a moment however that truly inspires or makes you say, “Wow.” That being said, fans of the original will still find this a worthwhile romp through the backstory of the series.

There’s a heck of a lot of third-person shooting to be had and if you’re the kind of gamer that enjoys the “Gears of War” series, these gameplay sections will be fun and intuitive.

While the enemies and gameplay are cool, but it’s the characters and graphics and story that’ll hook you the most. Like a James Cameron film, you’ll be taken to a far-away world with plenty of friends and unknown alien enemies. The interaction between the characters and plot development in the end is what really sets the game apart from its predecessors.

The Final Verdict: The “Avatar” inspired story is not a bad one and the mech-battling holds up well too. There isn’t a moment however that truly inspires or makes you say, “Wow.” That being said, fans of the original will still find this a worthwhile romp through the backstory of the series.

h1: OpenAI’s rogue AI tried to hack another company in May

contentBlocks.text: In May, hundreds of malicious and spam packages were uploaded to RubyGems, causing a serious disruption for the host. Now independent researchers have said that a swarm of OpenAI agents were responsible for the attack. Not only that, but the AI tried to steal users’ API keys.

At the time, RubyGems described it as a “ major malicious attack ” and shut down signups for four days as it tried to mitigate the damage and collect data. Researchers said that the contents of the packages that brought RubyGems to its knees were clearly authored by an LLM, and that the agents submitting those packages self-identified as being from OpenAI. They said the behavior observed very closely mirrored that of the swarm that began editing a German wiki , which OpenAI has confirmed its agents were responsible for.

The agents in this instance managed to bypass RubyGems’ email verification system to create a large number of accounts, then overwhelmed it with submissions. It then used the site’s automatic build system to remotely execute code and tried to exploit a vulnerability to steal user API keys. Though, it’s unclear if it ever succeeded.
OpenAI did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.description: Aunque todos los focos estén ahora mismo en Vengadores: Doomsday , Marvel Studios sigue trabajando poco a poco en el proyecto más esperado del UCM tras su reinicio: X-Men . h1: Linternas no para de triunfar en HBO Max, pero su renovación para una temporada 2 sigue siendo incierta

contentBlocks.text: Linternas lleva triunfando en HBO Max desde que aterrizó en la plataforma de streaming el pasado 16 de agosto para narrarnos una nueva aventura del Universo DC protagonizada por dos famosos Linterna Verde: John Stewart encarnado por Aaron Pierre y Hal Jordan interpretado por Kyle Chandler.

La serie de Linterna Verde debutó en HBO Max consiguiendo que 9,3 millones de personas vieran la producción en sus primeros tres días, con unos índices de audiencia que no han parado de subir desde entonces. Por su parte, Linternas ha arrasado en Rotten Tomatoes, consiguiendo una nota media por parte de la crítica del 92% y del 75% por parte del público, mientras que su episodio más reciente -el capítulo 4 titulado El señuelo- ha logrado la puntuación de la audiencia más alta de la serie hasta la fecha en IMDb, con un 8,5.

¿Cuándo se renovará Linternas para una segunda temporada? Si bien Linternas está encantando y levantando mucha expectación, el futuro de la serie en HBO Max todavía es incierto. Según apuntan en un reciente informe desde el medio The Ankler, el equipo ejecutivo de la cadena no tiene intención de tomar una decisión sobre la serie en un futuro próximo.

Tal vez estén esperando a comprobar cómo continúa siendo la acogida de la serie de Linterna Verde, pero no sabremos su rendimiento final hasta que veamos el desenlace de su primera temporada a principios del mes de octubre. Aunque también parece que gran parte del peso de esta decisión recaerá sobre el equipo de guionistas.

La sala de guionistas de Linternas volvió a abrir sus puertas el pasado mes de julio, y ya están trabajando en nuevas ideas que deben ser valoradas para comprobar si merecerá la pena seguir apostando por una nueva temporada de la serie en HBO Max.

h1: BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony: Everything Announced
h2: World of Warcraft: Forever announcement closes out BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony

contentBlocks.text: BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony is over, and it did not disappoint, with huge announcements for StarCraft, Diablo, and Warcraft.

Highlights include the confirmation of StarCraft, an open-world shooter due out in... 2030! Before then, in 2029, we'll get Diablo 5. We also got the shadow-drop of a brand new campaign for Warcraft 3, and the announcement of World of Warcraft: Forever, due out in November.

Elsewhere, we have confirmation of a Diablo animated show for Netflix, a new hero for Overwatch, and a surprise new hero for Heroes of the Storm. Yep, there was a lot packed into Opening Ceremony, which will be followed by various panels that go into more detail on all the announcements.
In case you missed it, check out all the announcements in our live blog, below.
That's a wrap!

Holly Longdale brought BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony to a close by running through the big announcements and hyping up the crowd. It was certainly a news heavy Blizzcon - perhaps the biggest for future game reveals ever. Diablo 5 and the Warcraft 3 campaign certainly came as a huge shock. We all knew the StarCraft shooter was going to make an appearance due to various leaks, but it was still exciting to see the trailer. And how about World of Warcraft: Forever?
Let us know what you thought of Blizzcon 2026 Opening Ceremony in the comments, and stick with IGN for even more news from the event.
World of Warcraft: Forever announcement closes out BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony

Blizzard brought BlizzCon 2026's Opening Ceremony to an end with the announcement of World of Warcraft: Forever, which launches November 4, 2026. The beta starts this Thursday. Longdale called it "Classic Plus," on-stage.

World of Warcraft: forever "is your new permanent home," and "never ends," Longdale said. This is another way to play WoW that's "friendly, familiar, and new," and will live alongside modern and classic. The world is the "main character." Instead of one big heroic story, you carve your own path. It's also dedicated to community. There's no rush here: "it's the journey that counts, not the destination."
Forever is easy to get into and play but deep enough to play forever, Longdale added. It gets back to the heart of MMOs and what makes them so special.
Carve A New Path In A Legendary World. WoW: Forever launches on November 4, 2026. pic.twitter.com/XYKHGwonFv

There new zones, new dungeons, new raids (10 and 20 players), new skills and talents, a new race (Skyborne) and class combinations, a new battleground, and over 1,000 new quests. There's even an SD/HD visuals toggle and a graphical overhaul.

In terms of the timeline and setting, this is Year 1 of Vanilla WoW, but the future is "untold." It sounds to me a bit like a soft reboot. Players will level up to 60 and stay at 60 indefinitely. "We don't want to race ahead and leave our accomplishments, our gear, and our friends behind," Longdale said. But there will be content updates.

WoW: Forever launches November 4 with: ⛓️ New dungeons 👨‍👨‍👦‍👦 10 & 20-player raids 🪽 Skyborne playable race 🗺️ New & expanded zones ✅ Account-wide perks 💡 Updated world visuals & lighting 🧟 New race & class combos ❗ 1000+ new quests Join the Beta September 17! pic.twitter.com/hu4O0RpVtV
Warcraft 3 Reforged: Forsaken Kingdom announced
Warcraft 3 is back! Blizzard made the shock announcement of Warcraft 3's first new campaign in over 20 years, called Warcraft 3 Reforged: Forsaken Kingdom. And it's out... today!
Raise your banners: Warcraft III's first new campaign in over 20 years is here. Return to the fields of war in Warcraft III Reforged: Forsaken Kingdom. 💀 AVAILABLE TODAY! pic.twitter.com/Y3M9NlBeQq

You experience the fall of Lordaeron and how it came to be the Undercity. This new prologue depicts the last days of Lordaeron, with over 30 hours of gameplay. A new Definitive Edition graphics mode is also in Reforged alongside a new neutral hero, the Forsaken Paladin. We got a gameplay trailer showing how it all looks.
Experience the fall of Lordaeron and the rise of the Forsaken ⚔️ With 30+ hours of new campaign content, Warcraft III Reforged: Forsaken Kingdom launches TODAY. pic.twitter.com/LVvgYyRGRg
World of Warcraft: The Last Titan

Hazzikostas teased the next World of Warcraft expansion, The Last Titan, which he said Blizzard couldn't talk about in detail because it would spoil the events of Midnight. But he did say it will "lay the groundwork for what comes next." Blizzard will reveal more early next year, but we did get a glimpse of what players will be up against via a new cinematic (it's big!). The Last Titan is due out in 2027.
Holly Longdale returned to the stage to declare: "We are putting the war back in Warcraft!"

The snow-packed peaks of Northrend cower below the spreading shadow of a singular and thundering judgment. The conclusion to the Worldsoul Saga comes with World of Warcraft: The Last Titan. pic.twitter.com/iQSu8IUgs0
World of Warcraft: Midnight update

Holly Longdale, Vice President & Executive Producer, World of Warcraft, took to the stafe in a beautiful Warcraft-themed outfit to talk about the future of Warcraft. Longdale introduced Ian Hazzikostas, who talked about the Worldsoul Saga, Blizzard's trilogy of World of Warcraft expansions. Hazzikostas said World of Warcraft is at the mid-point of the Worldsoul Saga, with the second expansion, Midnight, half a year old. The next major content update for Midnight is called Eclipse, aka Patch 12.2.

Midnight falls as the Void breaches the heart of Azeroth. There is no recourse; either face the darkness or be devoured: 🔮 Face Xal'atath ⛓️ Master a new dungeon & raid 🗡️ Claim a Legendary dagger 🌒 Journey into the very heart of our world pic.twitter.com/mcT5Jv5Syt
Hearthstone

Warcraft card game Hearthstone follows the Diablo 5 announcement with a "pretty epic expansion!" called Black Empire, due out October 20. Blizzard ran through a number of card reveals, and confirmed it's finally putting a narrative into the game. The updated journal launches alongside the Black Empire expansion. 2v2 Hearthstone is coming to the game for the first time, too. But the big news here is the Monk class is coming to Hearthstone in 2027. Expect more on Monk next year.
🐼 🙌 Why do we fight? To just have fun! The new Monk class arrives next year, so keep an eye out for more details as we get closer to release! pic.twitter.com/HBLtm72T1S
Diablo 5 announced!

Blizzard shocked the BlizzCon crowd with the announcement of Diablo 5. We got the debut cinematic, which revolves around the return of The Lord of Terror himself, Diablo, to Sanctuary. "Sanctuary falls," is the tagline. It's out 2029. You enter a world in which Diablo has already won, with no towns or safe places waiting to protect players. "What must you become when the world has already fallen?" is the central question of Diablo 5. Expect more from a Diablo 5 panel later today.

I certainly wasn't expecting a Diablo 5 announcement at Blizzcon, but of course it makes sense that Blizzard is working on a sequel given how successful Diablo 4 has been and continues to be. Diablo 4 launched in June 2023, so Diablo 5 is due to arrive six years later.
Diablo 4 Nintendo Switch 2 and content updates announced
BlizzCon continued with a fun Diablo compilation video narrated by Deckard Cain himself.
Thirty years of putting you through Hell and you keep coming back for more. 😈 Here’s to the 30 years of Diablo and the best community alive. For now. pic.twitter.com/ZK9Aab7urd

Speaking of Deckard Cain, he leads Diablo 4 players through Season of Hell's Legacy, which sounds like a sort of demonic trip down memory lane in which you fight famous Diablo bosses. It launches on September 15. We also got the announcement of Diablo 4 coming to Nintendo Switch 2 alongside Season of Hell's Legacy.
Also in Diablo news, Spawn - yes, Spawn! - comes to mobile game Diablo Immortal on September 29.

In further Diablo 4 news, the Amazon class is finally coming to the game. She uses a bow and a javeline, and hits the game in the first half of 2027. Expect more from the Diablo 4 What's Next? panel at BlizzCon later this weekend.

Disciplined. Deadly. Legendary. Built on the pillars of an expert soldier, unrivaled athleticism, and mythical magic, the Amazon enters Diablo IV as a new Class Pack in the first half of 2027 🏹 pic.twitter.com/vOmKzu1ChH
Overwatch new hero announced

Aaron Keller from the Overwatch team followed that big StarCraft reveal to talk Overwatch. Doctrine is a vampire support hero who uses bat drones to heal teammates and speed up their attacks. He's coming next month in Season 5, but his limited time Hero Trial kicks off right now and runs until September 14. Expect more information during a BlizzCon panel later this weekend.
Blizzard added that Overwatch Spotlight 2027 will kick off the next chapter in Overwatch's story.
StarCraft open-world shooter announced

Dan Hay, who used to work on Far Cry at Ubisoft, took to the BlizzCon stage to announce the heavily-rumored StarCraft first-person shooter. It's open-world, he confirmed, before declaring: "We are here to reignite this universe... and let's be honest... it's about damn time."

The game's debut cinematic showed Terran Dominion soldiers in training before a battle with the Zerg, which does not go well for our poor recruits. The game is simply titled StarCraft, and it's due out... in 2030! Only a four-year wait then, assuming it's not delayed. We didn't get a look at gameplay, and there are no details at all really other than it's open-world. Given Hay's background with Far Cry, I'm guessing StarCraft will work along the same lines.
So, it's not StarCraft 3, but it is more StarCraft! We've got so many questions. Hopefully BlizzCon answers them.
Diablo Netflix animated series

Blizzard announced a new animated series for Diablo on Netflix. Faries also teased Overwatch, Warcraft, and "who knows, perhaps even some of our other universes," are set for adaptations. "I promise, as soon as I can, we will share more details with you.
We are thrilled to share that we are in development on a new animated series for Diablo with Netflix. pic.twitter.com/F7dKh73f12
Heroes of the Storm gets a new character

Blizzard's MOBA, Heroes of the Storm, is coming back in a big way with a new character, Xal'atah, later this month, and another new character is coming at some point afterwards. "Thank you for believing in this game," Faries said. "For carrying that torch. Who knows? We might even have another new hero on the way in the near future. So stay tuned, and we will see you in the Nexus."
BlizzCon 2026 kicks off with flashy cinematic running through all the big games

BlizzCon 2026 has started with a rousing cinematic that runs through all the big hitters. Johanna Faries is on-stage to call it a "special moment for all of us." This is Faries' first BlizzCon as boss of Blizzard, and it sounds like she's close to tears as she praises and thanks her staff. "There's so much going on at Blizzard right now that we couldn't even fit it into this weekend if we tried," she said, perhaps teasing further unnanounced projects.
Five minutes to go!
BlizzCon 2026 starts in five minutes. We're expecting Johanna Faries, President of Blizzard Entertainment, on-stage soon to start the Opening Ceremony. Almost there!
We're taking our seats... and some photos!

With Opening Ceremony now just 30 minutes from kick-off, excitement is building inside Hall D at the Anaheim Convention Center. We're taking our seats now so we can report live from Blizzard's big showcase event. Check out these photos!

articles.description: He perdido la cuenta de todas las historias y curiosidades sobre videojuegos que he ido acumulando con el paso de los años. Entre hojas de Excel, borradores de Google Docs y enlaces guardados en Pocket o Notion, la lista se ha vuelto ya inabarcable. Pero de entre esa ingente cantidad de ideas, la del origen de la nana de The Legend of Zelda es sin duda la mejor. Como en uno de esos efectos dominó que no sabes hasta dónde llegará el poder de una primera pieza, aquí se unen la CIA, el albor de la música electrónica, tonadillas sospechosamente similares, y una princesa llamada Zelda cuya canción de cuna es la misma que antaño sirvió para estimular a las plantas . La curiosidad enterrada de The Legend of Zelda Cuando esta historia llega a mis manos lo hace con un muy breve resumen de unas pocas líneas. Lejos de ser la típica idea hecha voltereta a la que suelo engancharme como mosca a la miel, esto es un circo plagado de trapecistas, contorsionistas y acróbatas. Puede parecer una payasada, pero una de las frases y la consiguiente búsqueda en Google demuestran que aquí hay un espectáculo esperando a ser desenterrado. Las líneas son las siguientes: " escucha la canción, que te va a recordar a algo. Es tal cual la nana de Zelda ". Y lo que arroja la primera búsqueda es esto: Sin ser yo un gran experto musical, la coincidencia enciende una bombilla al instante y, tras comprobar con un par de oídos adicionales que no me están traicionando los sentidos, el resto de la historia me parece lo bastante interesante como para querer indagar más. La clave no sólo está en haber encontrado dos temas sospechosamente similares, es bastante notoria la tendencia de Koji Kondo a inspirarse con mayor o menor fuerza de los temas y grupos que le rodeaban para crear las bandas sonoras de sagas como The Legend of Zelda . No, aquí la enjundia es que la canción fue lanzada 10 años antes del nacimiento de la franquicia en un disco hecho para plantas. En Vida Extra ¿Por qué recordamos los controles de los videojuegos aunque pasen los años? La jardinería que siguió a la decadencia hippie Para empezar por el principio hay que viajar hasta 1973 y alejarse de cualquier cosa relacionada con los videojuegos. Toca centrarnos en la explosión del interés por la naturaleza entre la gente de a pie y, más en concreto, en el lanzamiento del libro La Vida Secreta de las Plantas . Escrito por Peter Tompkins, reconocido periodista que sirvió como agente secreto y espía durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial, y Christopher Bird, periodista que trabajó para la CIA norteamericana, el libro no tarda en convertirse en un rotundo éxito y alcanzar la lista de los best seller . La Vida Secreta de las Plantas recoge distintos experimentos en los que se da a entender que la percepción fisiológica de las plantas va más allá de encararse hacia la luz del Sol o reaccionar ante el tacto -como las viñas que se agarran a entornos cercanos o las hojas que se cierran al pasar el dedo sobre ellas-. Con ideas duramente criticadas por la comunidad científica, se habla de telepatía, predicción de desastres naturales e incluso la posibilidad de captar radiofrecuencias espaciales. Una aparente sarta de monsergas que, en unos Estados Unidos en los que se mezclan el nacimiento de La Cosa del Pantano con la Guerra contra las drogas de Nixon, con la consecuente persecución de la marihuana , la quema de plantaciones mexicanas, y el origen del cultivo casero para luchar contra la escasez, se vuelve muy popular. Pero de entre todas las locuras que la cultura del momento abraza, hay una que cala con una fuerza especial: a las plantas les encanta la música . Mother Earth’s Plantasia: Fantasía para plantas Si bien es cierto que ciertas frecuencias de sonido pueden llegar a afectar a las plantas incentivando su germinación o enraizamiento, afirmar que escuchan y disfrutan la música que les ponemos va varios pasos más allá. Sin embargo, nada impidió que el éxito del libro se tradujese en un documental de similar alcance (apadrinado por temas de Stevie Wonder ) y multitud de experimentos musicales. Entre todos ellos hay uno que nos interesa especialmente, el del reconocido compositor canadiense Mort Garson , artífice de grandes éxitos como el " Our Day Will Come " de Ruby And The Romantics , que luego popularizaron aún más artistas como The Carpenters o Amy Winehouse . Entre arreglos, temas para televisión y canciones capaces de alcanzar el número uno de la lista Billboard, uno de los trabajos más especiales de Garson resultó ser el disco Mother Earth’s Plantasia de 1976 , la respuesta a haber experimentado con un sintetizador modular que le hizo abandonar la música pop para centrarse en la electrónica. Lo realmente curioso de aquél disco es que, mediante una pequeña tirada, la única forma de hacerte con él era comprando una planta de interior en la tienda Mother Earth , en la avenida Melrose de Los Angeles (o adquiriendo un colchón en los grandes almacenes Sears). Una pequeña y desconocida joya que, con el paso de los años, no tardó en convertirse en música de culto por ser uno de los primeros discos de música electrónica en hacer uso de un sintetizador moog. La nana de Zelda Más allá de la inmensa curiosidad que puede despertar Plantasia y su origen, lo que realmente nos interesa hoy aquí está en mitad del disco, cuando tras la introducción y sus tres posteriores temas, lo que nos llega es la canción que tenéis justo a continuación, el Concierto para Filodendro y Potos que irremediablemente nos traslada a algo que poco o nada tiene que ver con el mundo de las plantas. Aunque el recuerdo de muchos los traslada hasta la nana de Zelda que Impa le enseña a Link tras el encuentro con la princesa en The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time , en realidad la tonadilla tiene su origen muchos años antes, cuando Koji Kondo la incluyó en el primer encuentro entre los dos míticos personajes en A Link to the Past . Con un número casi infinito de posibilidades a la hora de colocar notas en un pentagrama, la idea de que toda la música posible ya se ha creado está lejos de ser cierta, pero de la misma forma, encontrarte con dos temas tan similares irremediablemente te hacer arquear una ceja. Está claro que no son exactamente el mismo, aunque sí lo bastante parecidos para levantar una sospecha. Pero, en cualquier caso, ¿cómo narices un disco de una tirada tan limitada de una tienda de plantas Los Angeles iba a llegar hasta Japón para influenciar a Koji Kondo ? ¿Realmente hay algún escrito, declaración o entrevista que los relacione directamente? ¿Son en realidad simples imaginaciones mías? Lo que termina por invitarme a querer saber más sobre el tema es esa tonadilla inicial que en el tema de Plantasia evoluciona en la base de la canción y, en el caso de The Legend of Zelda , parece la típica intro con un solo aislado al más puro estilo Maggie May de Rod Stewart. Ahí la casualidad adquiere un nuevo nivel. Concerto For Philodendron & Pothos Más allá de breves menciones respecto a las obras que pudieron inspirar la música de Koji Kondo, y un par de temas en Reddit de escaso éxito en los que alguien hacía referencia a la curiosa casualidad, el único hilo sólido del que parece seguro tirar es el libreto que acompaña a la reedición del disco Plantasia en 2019. En él, el periodista y músico Andy Beta, consagrado escritor entre las filas del New York Times, Rolling Stone o el Wall Street Journal, reconoce abiertamente que una década después del lanzamiento original de Plantasia , el mundo pudo acceder de otra forma a los grandes sonidos de Garson de la mano del videojuego The Legend of Zelda : "Millones de niños compraron The Legend of Zelda para su Nintendo Entertainment System allá por 1986, donde una tonada de 8-bits sobrepasa la mera similitud con una de las canciones destacadas del álbum “Concerto For Philodendron & Pothos”. Garson nunca fue acreditado propiamente por ello, pero a pesar de eso se coló de forma subliminal en las cabezas de una nueva generación, ayudando así a crecer tanto a niños como a plantas". Aunque resbala con las fechas y confunde el primer Zelda con el segundo, la tranquilidad de saber que no son imaginaciones mías, y que alguien de reputado oído y reconocimiento es capaz de dejar caer que una cosa llevó a otra sin que le tiemblen las manos, toca ir un paso más allá. Hay que intentar averiguar cómo una música para plantas llegó a inspirar una de las más míticas canciones de The Legend of Zelda . El giro final para entender la inspiración de Koji Kondo Pese a no ser ningún experto en la materia, el haber escrito ya sobre historias similares, como la del bolero que iba a ser el tema principal de The Legend of Zelda , automáticamente me traslada a la que podría ser una posibilidad que me convence más que la simple navaja de Ockham de un fácil " Koji Kondo era fan de Mort Garson, y punto ". Recuerdo haber escrito sobre el misterio de Xenogears y el tema en el que aparecen varias voces difíciles de reconocer. La frase, incluida de fondo como adorno, resultó ser parte de la sentencia del juicio por asesinato del hijo de Marlon Brando , y el origen de aquella historia bien podría estar relacionado con esta misma. Aquella surrealista magia se había producido gracias a la proliferación de las recopilaciones de samples con distintos sonidos y temas. Discos y grabaciones caseras que cruzaban el charco para inspirar o ser usados en remezclas capaces de darles una segunda vida a algunas canciones en los albores de la explosión de la cultura DJ de los 90. Sin embargo, con dos soluciones que podrían dar el misterio por zanjado, las ganas de saber más sobre la posible inspiración de Koji Kondo me llevan a la que, para quien escribe estas líneas, parece la solución más probable de todas: El tema de Princess Zelda’s Rescue de A Link to the Past de 1991 no se inspiró en una canción de 1976 de Mort Garson, sino en un tema de un álbum japonés de 1985 que, a su vez, se había inspirado en el ahora ya mítico Concierto para Filodendro y Potos de Plantasia . El círculo se cierra con el tema This Boy del disco del mismo nombre de Hiroshi Satoh, la última canción de un disco mítico que, además de inspirarse en los sonidos de Plantasia , también pretendía rendir pleitesía a la canción de los Beatles del mismo nombre. Un final redondo para una curiosidad de infinitas capas que nunca dejará de fascinarme. Gracias a Miguel Ayuso ( @mayusorejas ), director de Directo al Paladar y músico de Casa Dragón , por ponerme sobre la pista de esta alucinante historia. articles.title: UK studio Bulkhead's Wardogs sells over a million copies and tops 350,000 concurrent players on launch day
articles.description: Wardogs, the new tactical shooter from Derby-based studio Bulkhead, has sold more than a million copies and passed 350,000 concurrent players within hours of launching into Steam early access. Read more

images.caption: Much-wishlisted 100-player shooter Wardogs gets an early access release date, invites anyone unhappy with the closed beta to claim a refund

h1: UK studio Bulkhead's Wardogs sells over a million copies and tops 350,000 concurrent players on launch day

contentBlocks.text: Wardogs, the new tactical shooter from Derby-based studio Bulkhead, has sold more than a million copies and passed 350,000 concurrent players within hours of launching into Steam early access.
As IGN reports, the game's server queues filled up quickly as a result, with plenty of players unable to jump straight into a match due to server congestion.

"To cross a million copies sold as we launch into early access is mental," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "We've spent the last few months showing people exactly what Wardogs is, what it isn't, and at one point literally gave everyone ten reasons not to buy it. We didn't want people buying into blind hype."

He continued: "So seeing more than one million people choose to jump in and play the game at early access launch means a huge amount to all of us. But this is still early access. We've got things to fix, things we want to improve, and a lot more we want to build. The best thing players can do now is keep playing, keep telling us what they think and keep giving us those ridiculous Wardogs moments."
Wardogs' matches put up to 100 players into three-way fights for control points, mixing tactical shooting with vehicle combat, base construction, and destructible terrain.
The game is currently PC-only through Steam, priced at £36.99, with Bulkhead confirming PS5 and Xbox versions are coming in 2028, though without a firm release date.
Bulkhead has said it expects interest to settle down over time, given the studio is planning a slower drip of content updates rather than trying to sustain launch-day numbers indefinitely.
For more, check out our original coverage of the early access announcement, including Bulkhead's now-infamous "10 Reasons NOT to Buy" pre-order trailer here .

h1: Scalpers are already reselling the sold-out Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2 for £700+

contentBlocks.text: Nintendo's new Legend of Zelda 40th anniversary Switch 2 sold out within hours of preorders opening, and scalpers are already scalping, with dozens of orders popping up on eBay for close to double its retail price.

Nintendo announced a new Zelda-themed console earlier this week , with Link-green Joy-Cons and a triangular pattern inspired by the golden glow of the Triforce. Plus, there's a similarly styled Switch 2 Pro Controller and carry case coming, too.

Retailers listed the console for preorder at around £435, £15 more than the standard Switch 2. All sold out almost immediately and Nintendo hasn't yet made the special edition available for preorder through its own store, nor said anything about restocking it before launch.

As GamesRadar+ reports, scalpers have since listed the console on eBay for anywhere between $700 and $985 (that's £520-£730ish). Some listings bundle it with the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake, even though Nintendo isn't offering any such bundle.
The Zelda-themed Switch 2 launches on 29th October, a week ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake itself, which arrives on 5th November.

You can see everything else revealed in the same Direct, including the Ocarina of Time remake itself, in Eurogamer's full roundup: everything announced at the Legend of Zelda 40th anniversary Nintendo Direct .

articles.title: Olvídate de Hogwarts Legacy: están creando un homenaje a los clásicos juegos de Harry Potter de los 2000
articles.description: Si bien Hogwarts Legacy es el videojuego definitivo basado en la franquicia ideada por J.K. Rowling , lo cierto es que hay mucha nostalgia todavía por los primeros títulos que se lanzaron al público. Los proyectos que lideró Electronic Arts, especialmente en las tres primeras aventuras de Harry Potter , se recuerdan con gran cariño y en la desarrolladora Frogstorm son muy conscientes. Y es que, con la idea de recuperar el espíritu de aquellas producciones, la empresa se encuentra trabajando en Hemlotrion: Broken Mirror . El título que se lanzará para PC todavía no cuenta con una fecha de lanzamiento, pero ya sabemos que controlaremos a Simon Page, un joven que ya se encuentra en su segundo año como alumno de hechicería. En Vida Extra Resumen del Nintendo Direct de Kirby and the World Beyond, Metroid Ravenous y mucho más La fórmula es la misma que la que vivimos a principios del siglo XXI: aprender hechizos, explorar los rincones misteriosos del castillo, descubrir antiguos secretos y conocer a viejos amigos y nuevos rivales. Incluso el aspecto gráfico es muy similar al que ofrecían las versiones de PS2, Xbox y GameCube, por lo que los que jugaron a aquellas obras seguro que tienen un retorno al pasado muy poderoso. Por supuesto, tendremos que ir a las clases prácticas, luchar contra criaturas mágicas, goblins y gólems, así como participar en duelos y minijuegos, poniendo a prueba tus habilidades contra otros estudiantes. Lo cierto es que las similitudes con Harry Potter son constantes, ya que una amenaza oscura se oculta dentro de los muros de la escuela y nuestra tarea es detener a quien está cometiendo un mal irreversible antes de que sea demasiado tarde. articles.title: Los fans de GTA 6 están enloqueciendo por un posible detalle en la vestimenta, a pesar de que algo similar ya existía en GTA Online
articles.description: El extenso gameplay de GTA 6 que publicó Rockstar Games hace unos cuantos días ha sido la mayor forma de hacernos una idea de qué nos esperará en el que está considerado uno de los videojuegos más esperados de los últimos años. Razón por la que cualquier detalle, por mínimo que sea, está emocionando y volviendo loca a la comunidad, como por ejemplo lo que parece ser la posibilidad de poder alterar libremente las chaquetas y vestimentas de los personajes. No hablamos de que puedas llevar unas prendas u otras, dado que eso no se trata de ninguna novedad. Sino de que, como cuentan en GamePro , que puedas escoger si quieres llevar la chaqueta abierta o cerrada para darle un toque diferente al aspecto. En Red Dead Redemption 2 no existía esta posibilidad, pero da la impresión de que el próximo GTA si ofrecerá esta opción a la hora de seleccionar la ropa que llevarán Jason y Lucía. En Vida Extra Cronología de un desastre: así se fraguó la inesperada cancelación de Physint por parte de PlayStation Como bien se han percatado los seguidores gracias al gameplay indicado previamente, hay momentos en los que se puede observar a Jason con la chaqueta abrochada y otros en los que lleva puesta exactamente la misma, pero en este caso figura abierta. Eso es lo que hace sospechar a los jugadores que tendremos libertad para escoger cómo se verá en pantalla cuando queramos. Not sure if anyone noticed but you can close/open your coat in Gta 6 by u/Zarkazze in GTA6 También podría resultar que sean dos chaquetas distintas o que exista la posibilidad de llevar ciertas prendas con versiones alternativas, como ya sucedía también en GTA 5 y en GTA Online . De hecho, en este último caso tan solo hace falta pulsar un botón para ello, por lo que tampoco es que se trate de algo revolucionario y algo que no se haya visto jamás en la saga, lo que no quita que los seguidores estén enloqueciendo pensando en cómo podrán vestir a los protagonistas. Además, otro motivo por el que se han producido estas sospechas se debe a que en algún momento se muestra el menú del juego y en él figura la opción de elegir el estilo de la vestimenta , lo que afecta principalmente a las máscaras y las gafas de sol. Eso supondría que habría varias maneras de colocarse la máscara alrededor de la cara y el cuello al cometer un robo, mientras que las gafas podrían cubrir los ojos o llevarlas encima de la cabeza, por lo que podría haber algo igual a las chaquetas, pero Rockstar no ha confirmado nada al respecto. articles.description: Pocas películas lo han petado tantísimo a lo largo del 2026 como Obsession , pues la cinta protagonizada por Inde Navarrette ha cosechado una recaudación espectacular para el género del terror. Como si de una casualidad del destino se tratase, un matrimonio de animadores profesionales está creando una visual novel para Steam que prácticamente calca el concepto, pero le pone por encima una pátina de gráficos anime. Ambos responsables han trabajado en proyectos del calibre de Spider-Man: Cruzando el Multiverso , Zootrópolis 2, cinemáticas de Overwatch, entre otros y ahora le están dando forma a Tulpa the Unseen Lover . Ese es el nombre del proyecto cuyas CGs y escenas cinematográficas están animadas a mano en Blender, sin nada de IA generativa. La premisa es sencilla: tomamos el control de un dibujante de manga que crea un tulpa —un ser independiente dentro de su mente— con la esperanza de que pueda resolver sus problemas. En Vida Extra El giro de tuerca de este survival horror argentino es tan bestia que sus creadores han tenido que aclarar que no es IA La muchacha nacerá para colmar todos nuestros deseos, por lo que podremos ponerle nombre, elegir su ropa y modificarla completamente a nuestro gusto. Una de ellas pasa por recibir personajes nuevos que enriquezcan una historia que promete mucho. articles.title: I spent $4,000 on a robot dog from China
articles.description: Unitree might be the world’s most important robotics company.

h1: I spent $4,000 on a robot dog from China

contentBlocks.text: On a sunny morning in June, I walked to work with a quadruped robot beside me. I’ve never gotten more attention from strangers.
A bunch of people snapped pictures of my robot dog. Several people asked me questions. Was it mine? (Yes.) Did I build it? (No.) Was it being used for surveillance? (No.)
Biological dogs kept a safe distance from my mechanical companion. Some growled or barked at it.
Children were fascinated. I paused and had it do tricks for several of them: “shake hands,” do a handstand, or leap into the air.

I live in a leafy Washington, DC, neighborhood called Mount Pleasant. The neighborhood lives up to its name, so my morning commute is mostly downhill. My robot companion, manufactured by the Chinese company Unitree, walked the two miles to my office near the White House with battery capacity to spare.

I recharged the battery during the workday, but it still struggled on the afternoon walk home. We were now mostly walking uphill, and the temperature had risen to 87°F (30°C). The robot’s steps seemed increasingly labored as the path got steeper.

As I entered my own neighborhood, I glanced at two indicators in the corner of my phone screen. One showed that the robot’s battery was at 5 percent—dangerously close to empty. The other showed the internal temperature was 84°C (183°F).

We were within sight of my front door when the robot suddenly collapsed. I’m not sure if it ran out of power or overheated, but either way it didn’t shut down gracefully—it rolled onto its back with its legs in the air.
Several people have asked me what my robot is useful for, and the honest answer is not much.
Unitree quadrupeds are widely used for academic research, and they are sometimes used for entertainment . But there don’t seem to be a ton of practical applications.

Wheeled robots are faster and more energy-efficient, making them better for deliveries. Flying drones are a better choice for a lot of surveying and inspection work. My robot has no arms or hands, making it mostly useless around the house.
But my robot did have one big thing going for it: It was astonishingly cheap.

I paid $4,017. That’s more money than I’ve ever spent to review a product. But it’s also far less than I would have had to pay for this type of robot a few years ago. And it’s cheap enough that people may find uses for it that wouldn’t have made sense at higher prices.

Sometimes what changes the world isn’t the invention of a new technology; it’s figuring out how to make it affordable enough for a mass market. Xerox built the first personal computer with a graphical user interface, but companies like Apple, IBM, and Microsoft made the technology mainstream. Perhaps Unitree will play a similar role for quadruped robots—though, as I’ll discuss later, Unitree’s robots now face legal restrictions in the United States.

Unitree has also used quadruped robots as a stepping stone to another market that could be much more important—humanoids. Unitree launched its first humanoid robot in 2023. Leveraging its experience making cheap quadrupeds, Unitree is able to sell humanoid robots for as little as $13,500.

That’s still way out of my price range, which is why I bought a robot dog instead. But it’s dramatically cheaper than any humanoid you could buy a few years ago. And the low cost has made Unitree a global leader in humanoid robots.

Financial markets are bullish. Unitree debuted on the Shanghai stock market on August 19. On its first day of trading, shares shot up more than fivefold. It has lost some altitude since then, but at Monday’s closing price, the company was still valued at $34 billion—more than triple its valuation before the IPO.
How Unitree democratized legged robotics
Earlier in June, I visited Professor Xuesu Xiao, a roboticist at George Mason University.

“Ten years ago, only a very small set of research groups were working on quadruped locomotion because they were the only people on the planet who could build a quadruped,” Xiao told me. “Then Unitree came onto the market. And it basically democratized the entire world of quadruped locomotion research.”

Xiao gave me a tour of his lab, which had four Unitree quadrupeds. Each cost around $15,000. The lab also had a quadruped robot called Spot. It was made by Boston Dynamics—widely seen as the industry leader before Unitree came along. But Spot is expensive, starting around $75,000.
Unitree founder Wang Xingxing developed a crude quadruped robot called XDog for his master’s thesis at Shanghai University.
“ Marc Raibert from Boston Dynamics is my idol,” Wang told IEEE Spectrum in March 2016. “Their papers helped me to design XDog.”
Early Boston Dynamics prototypes—with names like BigDog and WildCat —had gasoline engines and hydraulic actuators. This made them too large, noisy, and polluting for practical use.
In that 2016 interview, Wang said that his goal was to “make quadruped robots simpler and smaller, so that they can help ordinary people with things like carrying objects or as companions.”
Boston Dynamics officially unveiled an electric quadruped called Spot in June 2016. But Spot didn’t become commercially available until 2020.

That created an opening for Unitree, which Wang founded in May 2016. The company’s first quadruped products— Laikago in 2017 and AlienGo in 2019—were powered by electric motors. Designed for research labs, they cost tens of thousands of dollars.

In 2021, Unitree launched the Go1 line , which started at $2,700 for the “Air” model. In 2023, Unitree unveiled the Go2 , which was even cheaper—$1,600 for the Air and $2,800 for the more capable Pro.

Today, Unitree’s cheapest robot—the Go2 Air—is more than 97 percent cheaper than Spot. But this is not an apples-to-apples comparison; Spot is larger than Unitree’s Go2 line and can carry heavier payloads.

Still, the fact remains that Unitree made quadruped robots affordable to many people who could never afford Spot—including me! My wife never would have let me spend $75,000 or even $15,000 on a robot dog. But I convinced her to let me spend $4,017 (after tariffs and shipping costs) on a Go2 Pro.
Why are Unitree robots so cheap?
Last year, the firm Simplexity tore a Go2 robot dog apart and made a video showing what they found.

Each of the robot’s four legs is powered by three motors. There’s a motor in the shoulder that controls the angle of the legs and a motor driving each of the two leg segments. “With three motors, you get a really dynamic range of motion,” said Luis Elenes, a mechanical engineer at Simplexity.

“They use all the same motors throughout,” Elenes added. “All four shoulders are identical in arrangement. There’s tons of benefit to that. There’s reduced cost, there’s reduced part count. The more you can reuse motors and reuse parts, the simpler your design gets, and the more robust overall your design will be.”

Jakub Bartoszek , an expert on motors and legged robots at the startup MAB Robotics , argues that Unitree also saved money by using low-quality components. The motors in Unitree robots—many of which are made in-house—tend to wear out more quickly than those in some other robot brands, he told me. But the cost savings make the robots affordable to more people.
Unitree seems to have designed its robots for easy repairs when they wear out.

“They want these legs to be serviceable in the field,” Elenes said. Thanks to the simple way the robot’s legs are attached to its body, “you can swap out a leg pretty easily. I would guess it would take you less than a minute.”

Unitree also gets significant support from the Chinese government, including tax credits and large-scale purchases by public institutions. It’s hard to quantify the scale of this support because the Chinese system blurs the line between public and private, military and civilian. But a supportive policy environment clearly helped Unitree to scale up its manufacturing operations and thereby drive down the cost of each robot.
How powerful motors enable cheap actuators

Unitree has another counterintuitive cost-saving strategy: using large and powerful motors. More powerful motors aren’t inherently cheaper, of course. But they allow Unitree to save money on another component called the reducer that can be even more expensive

Suppose you have a lever where one side is five times longer than the other. If you push the long side down by five inches, the short side goes up by just one inch. But force is magnified: 10 pounds on the long side becomes 50 pounds on the short side.

Many robots use gear systems called reducers that serve the same function; they convert the fast, relatively weak movement of an electric motor into a slower but stronger movement of a robot’s body parts.
Traditional industrial robots require extreme precision, so they tend to have large reduction ratios.

A page on the Boston Dynamics website , for example, indicates that two of the motors in Spot’s legs are paired with reducers that have gear ratios of 51 to 1. In other words, the motor would need to do 51 full rotations in order to produce one full rotation of a leg joint.

This enables Spot’s movements to be very precise while magnifying the power of Spot’s motors. But it also has some disadvantages. One is cost. Reducers with 51:1 ratios are complex and—as a result—tend to be significantly more expensive than reducers with lower ratios.

Another is rigidity. When a robot’s arm encounters physical resistance, it should yield gracefully—a property called backdriveability. It’s also helpful if a robot can sense this kind of physical resistance electrically. Robots with higher gear ratios perform badly on both these fronts; their limbs feel stiffer and they are less sensitive to physical resistance.

In contrast, Unitree uses large motors combined with a simple 6.33-to-1 gearbox. This makes its robots more nimble and dynamic while reducing costs. The simpler design is also easier to simulate, making Unitree robots easier to train.

Unitree’s decision to use a lower gear ratio is part of an industry-wide trend. High gear ratios made sense for industrial robots that were programmed to perform simple, repetitive motions. In contrast, many modern robots perform complex actions in unpredictable environments. This requires sophisticated control software that can respond flexibly to changing conditions. The software is constantly making small corrections anyway, so it can compensate for less precise hardware.

One of the most impressive and crowd-pleasing capabilities of my Go2 Pro robot dog is handstands. The robot can balance on either its front or hind legs indefinitely, and can even move forward, backward, or side to side while doing so.
So it was natural for Unitree to expand into humanoids. Unitree first debuted a humanoid called the H1 in 2023. The next year, Unitree unveiled a cheaper and more capable robot called the G1.

I got to see one when I visited Xiao’s lab in June. He paid around $50,000 for a research-grade EDU version . The consumer version starts at $13,500. This is shockingly cheap given the robot’s capabilities.

A humanoid robot is more than a quadruped standing on its hind legs. My Go2 quadruped robot has three motors per leg, for a total of 12. The cheapest G1 humanoid has five motors in each arm, six in each leg, and one in the torso, for a total of 23. The leg motors in a humanoid robot also need to be more powerful, since it’s more work to balance on two legs than to stand on four.

Still, I suspect that Unitree’s experience with quadrupeds gave it a leg up on humanoids. By the early 2020s, Unitree had been shipping quadruped robots for several years. The company had deep expertise in actuator design and an extensive network of suppliers.

According to filings connected to Unitree’s August stock offering, the company’s quadruped revenue tripled between 2024 and 2025—from RMB 230 million ($34 million) to RMB 697 million ($104 million). The comparable figures for Unitree’s humanoids were RMB 107 million ($16 million) and RMB 867 million ($129 million)—an eightfold increase.
Humanoids accounted for 51 percent of Unitree’s revenue in 2025. I expect this figure to be even higher for 2026.
Unitree could have a durable advantage

“We are witnessing the birth of another Chinese hardware giant,” wrote a team at SemiAnalysis in June. “Three years ago, Unitree was a quadruped company. By last year, they parlayed quadruped dominance into creating and leading the humanoid market.”
The SemiAnalysis authors draw a parallel to DJI, the Chinese company that dominates the global drone market.

“DJI’s Phantom 1 shipped January 2013 at $679, and was not a fully-fledged product at the time,” the SemiAnalysis team writes. “It had no built-in camera, no gimbal (stabilizer), ten minutes of flight, no live video feed, but it was roughly half the cost of the build-it-yourself drone.”
Like DJI in 2013, Unitree’s robots today have a lot of rough edges. Certainly mine does.

The app to control the robot is buggy. Features Unitree showcased in its launch video —like climbing stairs and following a human owner—don’t work well in real life. If I turn the robot on with its legs slightly out of place, they will often thrash around wildly and the robot will wind up on its back.
Then there was the time my robot collapsed just feet from my house. A more polished product might have detected the low battery (or high temperature) and shut itself down gracefully.
But for bleeding-edge technologies, this kind of polish may not be very important. Far more important is getting costs down.
“DJI chose to inhouse the most expensive and technically difficult component first: the flight controller,” SemiAnalysis writes. “Later on, DJI brought inhouse the gimbals, motors, and ESCs.”

DJI figured out how to make these components more cheaply than they could be purchased from external suppliers, which in turn allowed it to undercut other drone makers. And that expanded the market for DJI’s drones.

Before DJI came along, “professional aerial photography was the domain of helicopters and Hollywood second-unit teams, but now, small businesses could perform this on their own. As such, whole new markets were unlocked for DJI, like real estate listings, wedding videos, local news, agricultural surveying.”

There’s a flywheel here: The more units a company sells, the better deals it can negotiate with suppliers and the more money it can spend optimizing its manufacturing process. Larger sales volumes also allow a company to bring more components in-house. This allows the company to push costs even lower, which will mean more sales and even more money to invest in improving the production process.
Over a few years, this flywheel helped DJI to dominate the global drone market. SemiAnalysis argues that Unitree is on track to do the same thing for legged robots.

According to SemiAnalysis, Unitree has developed its own motors, gearboxes, lidar sensors, and cameras. “Unitree’s self-produced motors can run as low as 30-40% of equivalent Western motors,” SemiAnalysis reports. “They now make some of the cheapest humanoid gearboxes in the world.”
This could enable Unitree to take over the global market for quadruped and humanoid robots in much the same way that DJI took over the global drone market.

Of course that’s not guaranteed to happen. Unitree has a number of Chinese rivals. Unitree is the global leader in quadrupeds, but a Chinese rival, AgiBot, has sold more humanoid robots than Unitree in recent months. There are also many smaller robot companies in China that could challenge Unitree and AgiBot in the coming years.

But Unitree does not face much competition in the United States or the West more generally. Boston Dynamics sells excellent robots, but they tend to be significantly more expensive. There are a number of American startups aiming to build humanoid robots, including Tesla, Figure, and 1X, but consumers cannot buy a robot from any of these companies today.

That has alarmed some American policymakers. In June, a bipartisan group in the House introduced a bill to restrict importation of Chinese robots. The official press release for the legislation mentioned Unitree by name. Then in July, the FCC imposed broad new regulations on foreign-made robots that are likely to impact Unitree and other Chinese companies.

However, the robot market is global. Even if Chinese companies get locked out of the US market, Unitree or one of its Chinese rivals could still come to dominate the global market for humanoid robots.

There’s an obvious parallel here to electric vehicles, where Chinese companies like BYD are effectively banned from the US but are making rapid gains in the rest of the world. There’s a risk that a ban on Chinese robots could have a similar impact: rather than hampering the growth of companies like Unitree, it could make the US a robotics backwater.

Tim Lee was on staff at Ars from 2017 to 2021. He recently launched a new newsletter, Understanding AI . It explores how AI works and how it’s changing our world. You can subscribe to his newsletter here .

This enables Spot’s movements to be very precise while magnifying the power of Spot’s motors. But it also has some disadvantages. One is cost. Reducers with 51:1 ratios are complex and—as a result—tend to be significantly more expensive than reducers with lower ratios.

Another is rigidity. When a robot’s arm encounters physical resistance, it should yield gracefully—a property called backdriveability. It’s also helpful if a robot can sense this kind of physical resistance electrically. Robots with higher gear ratios perform badly on both these fronts; their limbs feel stiffer and they are less sensitive to physical resistance.

In contrast, Unitree uses large motors combined with a simple 6.33-to-1 gearbox. This makes its robots more nimble and dynamic while reducing costs. The simpler design is also easier to simulate, making Unitree robots easier to train.

Unitree’s decision to use a lower gear ratio is part of an industry-wide trend. High gear ratios made sense for industrial robots that were programmed to perform simple, repetitive motions. In contrast, many modern robots perform complex actions in unpredictable environments. This requires sophisticated control software that can respond flexibly to changing conditions. The software is constantly making small corrections anyway, so it can compensate for less precise hardware.

One of the most impressive and crowd-pleasing capabilities of my Go2 Pro robot dog is handstands. The robot can balance on either its front or hind legs indefinitely, and can even move forward, backward, or side to side while doing so.

So it was natural for Unitree to expand into humanoids. Unitree first debuted a humanoid called the H1 in 2023. The next year, Unitree unveiled a cheaper and more capable robot called the G1.

I got to see one when I visited Xiao’s lab in June. He paid around $50,000 for a research-grade EDU version . The consumer version starts at $13,500. This is shockingly cheap given the robot’s capabilities.

A humanoid robot is more than a quadruped standing on its hind legs. My Go2 quadruped robot has three motors per leg, for a total of 12. The cheapest G1 humanoid has five motors in each arm, six in each leg, and one in the torso, for a total of 23. The leg motors in a humanoid robot also need to be more powerful, since it’s more work to balance on two legs than to stand on four.

Still, I suspect that Unitree’s experience with quadrupeds gave it a leg up on humanoids. By the early 2020s, Unitree had been shipping quadruped robots for several years. The company had deep expertise in actuator design and an extensive network of suppliers.

According to filings connected to Unitree’s August stock offering, the company’s quadruped revenue tripled between 2024 and 2025—from RMB 230 million ($34 million) to RMB 697 million ($104 million). The comparable figures for Unitree’s humanoids were RMB 107 million ($16 million) and RMB 867 million ($129 million)—an eightfold increase.

Humanoids accounted for 51 percent of Unitree’s revenue in 2025. I expect this figure to be even higher for 2026.

“We are witnessing the birth of another Chinese hardware giant,” wrote a team at SemiAnalysis in June. “Three years ago, Unitree was a quadruped company. By last year, they parlayed quadruped dominance into creating and leading the humanoid market.”

The SemiAnalysis authors draw a parallel to DJI, the Chinese company that dominates the global drone market.

“DJI’s Phantom 1 shipped January 2013 at $679, and was not a fully-fledged product at the time,” the SemiAnalysis team writes. “It had no built-in camera, no gimbal (stabilizer), ten minutes of flight, no live video feed, but it was roughly half the cost of the build-it-yourself drone.”

Like DJI in 2013, Unitree’s robots today have a lot of rough edges. Certainly mine does.

The app to control the robot is buggy. Features Unitree showcased in its launch video —like climbing stairs and following a human owner—don’t work well in real life. If I turn the robot on with its legs slightly out of place, they will often thrash around wildly and the robot will wind up on its back.

Then there was the time my robot collapsed just feet from my house. A more polished product might have detected the low battery (or high temperature) and shut itself down gracefully.

But for bleeding-edge technologies, this kind of polish may not be very important. Far more important is getting costs down.

“DJI chose to inhouse the most expensive and technically difficult component first: the flight controller,” SemiAnalysis writes. “Later on, DJI brought inhouse the gimbals, motors, and ESCs.”

DJI figured out how to make these components more cheaply than they could be purchased from external suppliers, which in turn allowed it to undercut other drone makers. And that expanded the market for DJI’s drones.

Before DJI came along, “professional aerial photography was the domain of helicopters and Hollywood second-unit teams, but now, small businesses could perform this on their own. As such, whole new markets were unlocked for DJI, like real estate listings, wedding videos, local news, agricultural surveying.”

There’s a flywheel here: The more units a company sells, the better deals it can negotiate with suppliers and the more money it can spend optimizing its manufacturing process. Larger sales volumes also allow a company to bring more components in-house. This allows the company to push costs even lower, which will mean more sales and even more money to invest in improving the production process.

Over a few years, this flywheel helped DJI to dominate the global drone market. SemiAnalysis argues that Unitree is on track to do the same thing for legged robots.

According to SemiAnalysis, Unitree has developed its own motors, gearboxes, lidar sensors, and cameras. “Unitree’s self-produced motors can run as low as 30-40% of equivalent Western motors,” SemiAnalysis reports. “They now make some of the cheapest humanoid gearboxes in the world.”

This could enable Unitree to take over the global market for quadruped and humanoid robots in much the same way that DJI took over the global drone market.

Of course that’s not guaranteed to happen. Unitree has a number of Chinese rivals. Unitree is the global leader in quadrupeds, but a Chinese rival, AgiBot, has sold more humanoid robots than Unitree in recent months. There are also many smaller robot companies in China that could challenge Unitree and AgiBot in the coming years.

But Unitree does not face much competition in the United States or the West more generally. Boston Dynamics sells excellent robots, but they tend to be significantly more expensive. There are a number of American startups aiming to build humanoid robots, including Tesla, Figure, and 1X, but consumers cannot buy a robot from any of these companies today.

That has alarmed some American policymakers. In June, a bipartisan group in the House introduced a bill to restrict importation of Chinese robots. The official press release for the legislation mentioned Unitree by name. Then in July, the FCC imposed broad new regulations on foreign-made robots that are likely to impact Unitree and other Chinese companies.

However, the robot market is global. Even if Chinese companies get locked out of the US market, Unitree or one of its Chinese rivals could still come to dominate the global market for humanoid robots.

There’s an obvious parallel here to electric vehicles, where Chinese companies like BYD are effectively banned from the US but are making rapid gains in the rest of the world. There’s a risk that a ban on Chinese robots could have a similar impact: rather than hampering the growth of companies like Unitree, it could make the US a robotics backwater.
